newsitem.title: USA: Swiss banks face tough audit on Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks face tough audit on Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Forensic auditors with the ability to penetrate Swiss banking secrecy will soon begin a full-scale investigation of all institutions believed to be holding dormant Holocaust-era accounts, a U.S. congressional panel heard on Wednesday.

Former Federal Reserve Board Chairman Paul Volcker, who heads a special commission set up by Switzerland and Jewish groups to determine the extent of Holocaust-era deposits, said there would be "hundreds of auditors crawling through these banks" by this fall.
"There will be no legitimate place for the audited banks to hide from our investigation," he told the House Banking and Financial Services Committee.

Volcker, in a simultaneous announcement with his counterpart in Switzerland, also said that Swiss banks had agreed to set up an independent panel to resolve claims to funds deposited by Jews murdered by the Nazis.
In addition, the banks would publish worldwide the names of foreign dormant accounts on July 23 and a second list of Swiss dormant accounts on Oct. 20.

Volcker described the audit of Swiss banks -- which will be carried out by three large international accounting groups -- as unprecedented in terms of normal banking practices and particularly so in the case of Switzerland, which is especially sensitive to the privacy of its financial institutions.
The target date for completion of the investigation is late 1998, although Volcker said he expected to report "significant concrete progress" by the end of this year.
But the news failed to mollify some members of the committee, who accused the Swiss government and the country's banks of anti-Semitism, stalling and empty promises.
"Switzerland's credibility is beginning to resemble the country's famous namesake cheese," Representative Rick Lazio told the hearing.

The New York Republican said all the promises made by the Swiss were empty because Holocaust survivors "haven't seen one franc." He called for an honest accounting instead of the "obscene outburts of anti-Semitism we have heard from the highest levels of their government and banking industry."
Representative Sue Kelly, Republican of New York, called the Holocaust-era assets held by Swiss banks "blood money" and urged the resolution of claims as soon as possible.

Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee and the primary congressional force behind the push to ascertain the fate of assets of Holocaust victims, accused the Swiss of "running out the clock" on the issue.
"This lack of action seems to be an effort to stall the truth, to stall justice from being achieved," the New York Republican said.
Swiss Ambassador Thomas Borer, who heads a task force set up by Switzerland to deal with the controversy, outlined the steps his country was taking to resolve the issue and pledged quick action.

"Time is critical for the survivors of the Holocaust and all those who can claim assets still kept in Switzerland," he said. "We shall see to it, as the studies proceed, solidarity and restitution will not incur further delay."
